auxiliary_passages.statement_original: Concretely, let $\omega>0$ define the ratio between the cost of each false discovery and the benefit of each true discovery. Then the utility of making $R$ rejections, of which $V$ are false discoveries, is proportional to $(R-V)-\omega V$, and a simple calculation shows that we should reject the $i$th hypothesis if and only if $\operatorname{lfdr}(p_i)\leq\alpha:=\frac1{1+\omega}$.

evidence.location: Introduction — cost ratio and target level

auxiliary_passages.resolution: The target alpha is fixed by omega>0 and lies in (0,1). Ell is the SL tuning parameter; lambda is the upper order-statistic cutoff; neither is the same parameter as alpha. In Theorem 6, ell=alpha/pi_0 and the data-dependent level is alpha/pi-hat_0.

auxiliary_passages.statement_original:
Throughout this section, we will restrict our attention to procedures that reject the $R$ hypotheses with the smallest $p$-values. That is, we assume a procedure $\mathcal R$ rejects $H_{(1)},\ldots,H_{(R)}$, where $H_{(k)}$ represents the hypothesis corresponding to $p_{(k)}$. If $f_1$ is non-increasing, then the procedure’s last rejection $H_{(R)}$ is the least promising, and the max-lfdr can be equivalently characterized as the probability that the last rejection is a false discovery:
\[
\operatorname{max\text{-}lfdr}(\mathcal R)=\mathbb E\left[\operatorname{lfdr}\big(p_{(R)}\big)\cdot\mathbf1\{R>0\}\right]=\mathbb P\{H_{(R)}=0,R>0\}.\tag{10}
\]

evidence.location: Section 1.2 — sorted hypothesis labels and last-rejection identity

auxiliary_passages.resolution: H_(k) follows the same ordering permutation as p_(k). Under the continuous-density model ties have probability zero. R=0 contributes zero, consistent with D4. Theorem 1 separately establishes the last-rejection identity without requiring monotonicity; only the max-lfdr identification uses D3.

auxiliary_passages.statement_original:
By comparison, the population version of our procedure $\tau_\ell$ is
\[
t_\ell:=\sup\left\{t\in[0,1]:t\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{s\in[0,1]}\{F(s)-s/\ell\}\right\},
\]
which coincides with the oracle threshold $\tau^*$ when $\ell=\alpha/\pi_0$.
auxiliary_passages.resolution: This binds the source t_ell notation. Under Theorem 5, its unique interior crossing f(t_ell)=1/ell, monotonicity and negative local derivative identify this population optimizer. It is distinct from the random threshold tau_ell=p_(R_ell). Theorem 5 states the crossing and uniqueness explicitly, so this alternative characterization is auxiliary rather than an extra extracted interface.

auxiliary_passages.statement_original:
For $t\in[0,1]$, let $\mathcal R_t^{\mathrm{Fix}}:=\{i:p_i\leq t\}$, and note that the oracle method is $\mathcal R^*=\mathcal R_{\tau^*}^{\mathrm{Fix}}$ where $\tau^*$ is the oracle threshold (7). We introduce the function $\rho(t)$ to represent the regret of this method, which is free of $m$:
\[
\rho(t):=\operatorname{Regret}_m(\mathcal R_t^{\mathrm{Fix}})=F(\tau^*)-F(t)-\frac{\pi_0}{\alpha}(\tau^*-t).\tag{17}
\]
auxiliary_passages.resolution: Theorem 6 uses the expected excess risk D10 for a threshold selected from the same data. It does not define this risk as E[rho(tau)] using a fixed-threshold population expression. Formula (17) is archived to preserve that distinction and is not added as a statement prerequisite.

auxiliary_passages.statement_original: The method $\mathcal R_\alpha^\lambda$ coincides with $\mathcal R_{\alpha/\widehat\pi_0^\lambda}$, our original procedure applied at the corrected level $\widehat\ell=\alpha/\widehat\pi_0^\lambda$, whenever $\tau_{\widehat\ell}\leq\lambda$.

evidence.location: After Theorem 4 — constrained versus unconstrained rule

auxiliary_passages.resolution: The agreement is conditional on the unconstrained threshold lying below lambda. Theorem 4 concerns the constrained rule, while Theorem 6 concerns the ordinary SL rule at a general estimated level. The specific estimator (12) is not a requirement of Theorem 6.

auxiliary_passages.statement_original: By specializing Theorem 5 to $\ell=\alpha/\pi_0$ and $\widehat\ell=\alpha/\widehat\pi_0$, we obtain the limiting regret for our procedure with a known or accurately estimated null proportion.

evidence.location: Before Theorem 6 — change of tuning parameter

auxiliary_passages.resolution: This gives the source correspondence between the two asymptotic results. Theorem 6 states its own three conditions, including a one-sided estimator error bound. It does not explicitly inherit Theorem 5(iii) or replace its own condition by a two-sided one. The mismatch is recorded separately.

auxiliary_passages.statement_original: The density estimator $\widehat f_m$ may be efficiently computed via the pool adjacent violators algorithm (see, e.g., Robertson et al., 1988, Chapter 1), but the definition of $\mathcal R_\ell$ in (4) provides a way to characterize and run our procedure without explicitly computing $\widehat f_m$.

evidence.location: Grenander estimator discussion — source implementation distinction

auxiliary_passages.resolution: The Grenander estimator and least concave majorant are used to analyze the rule, but none of the four Theorem statements requires their construction to define its objects. They are not included as proof-only interfaces. The direct SL definition D5 resolves the empirical threshold.

standard_ambient_resolution.shared: D1 fixes an iid two-groups experiment of size m: H_i=0 is a true null, H_i=1 a non-null, conditional p-values have densities f_h on [0,1], and the null is uniform. The marginal f and cdf F are in D1. All expectations and probabilities average both H and p under this model, unless the text explicitly conditions. H denotes the whole binary vector. D5 defines sorted p-values, p_(0)=0, the last-minimizer convention, the rejection count R_ell, set R_ell in calligraphic type and threshold tau_ell. A2 defines H_(k). Standard ambient objects include indicator functions, finite maxima, order statistics, conditional probability versions, expectation, variance, Bernoulli laws, differentiability, probability/distribution limits and deterministic little-o. In the asymptotic sections the mixture parameters and densities are fixed as m grows. A1 fixes omega>0 and alpha=1/(1+omega); ell is a tuning level and lambda a cutoff, while epsilon is an arbitrary positive tail tolerance.
standard_ambient_resolution.1: D1 resolves model (1), the uniform null and pi_0 in [0,1]. D5 resolves procedure (4), R_ell and its last-rejection threshold, with ell<=1 as printed and the nonnegative-level interpretation from context. A2 resolves the reordered label H_(R_ell); the guard R_ell>0 prevents a nonexistent rejection from contributing. D2 defines lfdr. The first exact identity does not require D3. Only the final sentence additionally requires non-increasing f_1, so D4 max-lfdr equals the last-rejection quantity. No BH procedure, null-proportion estimator, Chernoff distribution or loss function is required.
standard_ambient_resolution.4: D1 and D3 give the two-groups model, uniform null and non-increasing alternative. Lambda is fixed in (0,1). D8 is pi-hat_0^lambda from (12), including the plus one and the strict count p_i>lambda. The theorem binds the constrained index and rejection set inline; D9 retains those definitions and D5 supplies the order-statistic and last-minimizer conventions. D4 is the expected maximum lfdr with zero for no rejection. A5 records the conditional relation to the ordinary estimated-level rule, without replacing the constrained procedure. The estimator asymptotics on page 11 are not assumptions of this finite-sample result.
standard_ambient_resolution.5: D1,D3 fix the iid uniform-null mixture with pi_0 strictly between zero and one and a non-increasing alternative. Ell is fixed in (0,1/pi_0). The theorem itself binds the unique interior t_ell satisfying f(t_ell)=1/ell, requires C1 regularity near t_ell and f-prime(t_ell)<0, and quantifies any random ell-hat with m^(1/3)(ell-hat-ell) tending to zero in probability. A3 connects t_ell to the population optimizer; D5 defines the data threshold tau_(ell-hat), and D2 its lfdr. D11 defines Z as the maximizer location of unit two-sided Brownian motion minus t squared. The two distributional limits are followed by the additional tail condition (25), then mean convergence and both variance limits. The printed negative exponent in (25) is retained. No particular null-proportion estimator or Grenander implementation is imposed.
standard_ambient_resolution.6: D1,D3 fix the iid mixture with pi_0 in (0,1), uniform null and non-increasing alternative. A1 fixes the cost-derived alpha. D2 and D7 resolve lfdr and the oracle tau*, which this theorem additionally binds as a unique interior crossing lfdr(tau*)=alpha, with C1 density near tau* and negative derivative. The estimator pi-hat_0 is arbitrary subject to the original one-sided condition (iii); it is not necessarily D8 and is not silently assumed to satisfy a two-sided bound. D5 defines ordinary SL at alpha/pi-hat_0. D10 defines the unconditional empirical Bayes regret through weighted loss D6 and oracle D7, not the population fixed-threshold proxy in A4. D11 supplies the same Chernoff variable Z and its variance. The conclusion is deterministic convergence of the scaled expected regret with the exact printed -1/3 coefficient. A6 preserves the preceding specialization explanation without adding hypotheses to the theorem.

unresolved_source_conventions.note: The abstract describes lfdr as the probability that a null hypothesis is false. Equation (2) explicitly defines it as P(H_i=0 | p_i=t), meaning the null is true. The actual definition is preserved; the abstract wording is not used to reverse the event.

The density-ratio formula is a version of a conditional probability given a continuously distributed p-value. Pointwise values at zero-density points are not specified; the endpoint pi_0=0 can produce 0/0 away from the support. The max-lfdr definition assigns zero to an empty set, and the empty-rejection term in (11) must likewise be read as zero without evaluating an undefined H_(0).

Non-increasing f_1 gives the required non-decreasing lfdr in the nondegenerate mixture setting. The converse need not identify the shape of f_1 when pi_0 is 0 or 1. The source equivalence is preserved, and Theorems 5/6 explicitly restrict pi_0 to (0,1).

The last-minimizer rule and p_(0)=0 are explicit. Theorem 1 prints ell<=1 without an explicit lower bound; Theorem 4 does not print an ell range. Ell is used as a nonnegative testing level in context. The constrained rule uses p_(k)<=lambda despite the prose below lambda. The k>=0 range implicitly ends at m because only m order statistics exist. No change is made to either original statement.

Equation (7) uses a maximum and a weak lfdr inequality under monotonicity, without a global continuity or endpoint-version condition that always guarantees attainment. Theorems 5/6 add unique interior crossings and local smoothness, avoiding an ambiguous threshold in their own setting. The empty-set convention remains tau*=0.

Assumption (iii) uses m^(1/3)(ell-hat-ell) converging to zero in probability. The additional condition (25) instead prints m^(-1/3)|ell-hat-ell| inside a tail probability. That weaker-looking exponent is preserved exactly; no expected positive exponent is substituted for it.

The source requires only P{m^(1/3)(pi-hat_0-pi_0)>epsilon}=o(m^(-2/3)), without an absolute value or a lower-tail condition. This alone does not imply two-sided consistency, despite the preceding specialization discussion. A two-sided condition is not silently imported from Theorem 5.

The explicit estimator (12) is strictly positive but may exceed one, and no clipping is specified. Theorem 6 allows any estimator under its printed one-sided condition, without separately requiring pi-hat_0>0; alpha/pi-hat_0 therefore needs a convention if it is zero. Theorem 5 likewise does not specify a domain for the random ell-hat. These omissions are recorded instead of supplying an unstated truncation.

The proofs of Theorems 4 and 5 and the asymptotic analysis are deferred to Appendix A. Only its heading crop was inspected. All objects required to state the saved Theorems are resolved from the main text; no appendix proof assumptions are imported.
